1:
The chronicler opens the reign of Manasseh almost exactly where the older history left it, and the witnesses notice the near-identity of the two records at once. The reformed John Gill observes that from this point to the end of the chapter the same events are set down, well-nigh word for word, as in the parallel at 2 Kings 21, and is content to send the reader there for the fuller detail. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry agrees that the narrative of this great wickedness is the same, almost verbatim, with what had already been read and mourned over at 2 Kings 21:1-9, and confesses it no such pleasing subject that we should delight to dwell upon it again.

But the bare notice that Manasseh came to the throne a boy of twelve and reigned five and fifty years sets the witnesses pondering the mystery of a godly father's ungodly son. Henry paints him as a foolish young prince who, in flat contradiction to the good example and the good education his father Hezekiah had given him, abandoned himself to all impiety, transcribed the abominations of the heathen, ruined the established religion, and unravelled his father's glorious reformation. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, surveying the whole reign — its fifty-five years, its restored idolatry, its polluted temple, its captivity and its repentance — fastens on the same painful riddle. Manasseh, he grants, had no godly director once Hezekiah was gone, and his youth was therefore the more easily seduced; "but surely he had a pious education," Clarke presses; "how then could the principles of it be so soon eradicated?"

The witnesses do not answer the riddle by softening it. Henry draws from it three sober lessons: that it is no new thing, but a very sad one, for the children of godly parents to turn aside from the good way of God in which they have been trained, for parents may give their children many good things but cannot give them grace; that corruptions in worship are diseases the church is very apt to relapse into even when they seem cured; and that the god of this world has strangely blinded men's minds, drawing them from God their best friend to lean upon their sworn enemy. Gill and Clarke fix the near-identity of the record and the puzzle of the young king's swift fall; Henry reads in it the whole tragic pattern of inherited privilege despised. Between them they set the frame for all that follows — a boy reared in the light of Hezekiah's reforms who would plunge his kingdom into a darkness deeper than the heathen's, and yet, before the chapter closed, be dragged by affliction back to the God of his father.
2:
The verdict of condemnation falls at once — Manasseh did the evil that was in the sight of the LORD, "after the abominations of the heathen, whom the LORD had cast out before the children of Israel" — and the witnesses weigh both the standard by which he is judged and the reversal it implies. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch take the verse as the head of the whole indictment that runs through the verses following, where the catalogue unfolds: he built again the high places, reared altars for the Baalim, made groves, and worshipped and served all the host of heaven. The measure of his evil is not Israel's own earlier lapses but the abominations of the very nations God had dispossessed to plant his people in the land; Manasseh, in effect, morally undoes the conquest, making Judah like the Canaanites whom the LORD had swept out before them.

The reformed John Gill glosses the evil in his customary single stroke: it was idolatry, the same in substance as the account already given at 2 Kings 21, to which he refers the reader. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sharpens the tragedy of it: this young prince transcribed the abominations of the heathen, ruined the established religion, and unravelled his father's glorious reformation. What Hezekiah had built up with such labour — purging the temple, breaking the images, cutting down the groves — his son pulled down; the reformation of one reign became the plaything of the next.

From this Henry draws the melancholy observation that governs the whole chapter: that corruptions in worship are such diseases of the church as it is very apt to relapse into again, even when they seem to have been cured. The cleansing of the sanctuary under Hezekiah had not killed the appetite for idols; it had only suppressed it, and under a pliant boy-king that appetite broke out worse than before. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the sin as idolatry and points to the parallel; Keil sets the verdict at the head of the catalogue and marks the damning comparison with the dispossessed heathen; Henry reads in it the swift ruin of a father's reforms and the church's fatal proneness to relapse. Between them they show that the "evil in the sight of the LORD" was no private vice but a public apostasy, measured against the very abominations for which God had emptied the land, and now welcomed back into it by the hand of a king who should have known better. The judgment is severe precisely because the light against which Manasseh sinned was so bright.
3:
The catalogue of restored idolatry begins, and the witnesses trace each object of Manasseh's worship. He "built again the high places which Hezekiah his father had broken down," reared altars for the Baalim, made groves, and worshipped all the host of heaven. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke identifies the several cults: the Baalim he takes for the sun and moon, the "groves" for Asheroth — that is Astarte, or Venus — and the host of heaven for all the planets and stars. Manasseh, on this reading, imported the whole apparatus of astral and nature worship, bowing to the lights of heaven and the goddess of fertility together.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott refines the grammar of the plurals. "The Baals," he notes, are the different images of Baal, and the "groves" are properly Asheras — where the older account at 2 Kings 21 has the singular, the chronicler's plural is rhetorical, meaning that Manasseh made such things as Asheras; and Kings adds pointedly that he made them "as Ahab king of Israel made," so that a king of David's line now aped the worst apostasy of the northern throne. His fellow grammatical-historical witness Keil and Delitzsch simply set the whole roll in order — the high places rebuilt, the altars for Baalim, the groves, the host of heaven worshipped and served — as the systematic reversal of the father's reform.

That reversal is the point on which the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells: here Manasseh "ruined the established religion" and "unravelled his father's glorious reformation." Hezekiah had broken down these very high places, as the chronicler had recorded of his zeal; and now the son rebuilds precisely what the father had demolished, stone by stone, as though setting himself deliberately against his father's God. The witnesses do not divide. Clarke names the deities behind the terms, Ellicott secures the force of the plurals and the damning comparison with Ahab, Keil marks the ordered advance of the apostasy, Henry the deliberate undoing of the reformation. Between them they portray a young king not merely drifting into idolatry but reconstructing it with method — high place, altar, grove, and star — and matching, in the very city of David, the idolatry that had already destroyed the ten tribes. The rebuilding of Hezekiah's ruins is itself a kind of sermon in reverse: what one generation tears down in obedience, the next may raise again in rebellion, and the labour of reform is never so secure that a single wicked reign cannot overthrow it.
4:
The apostasy now invades the sanctuary itself, and the witnesses feel the peculiar affront of it: Manasseh "built altars in the house of the LORD, whereof the LORD had said, In Jerusalem shall my name be for ever." To rear pagan altars anywhere was sin; to rear them in the one house God had claimed as the dwelling of his name is a defiance of a wholly different order. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks the precedent and the aggravation. Manasseh built altars in the Temple, he observes, exactly as Ahaz had done before him — the wicked grandfather's pattern reappearing in the grandson, so that the altar Ahaz copied from Damascus at 2 Kings 16:10 has its counterpart here. And Ellicott notes a small but pointed heightening in the chronicler's language: where the older record had God say only "I will set my name," the chronicler writes "shall my name be for ever" — a stronger claim, and so a sharper indictment of the man who profaned it.

His fellow grammatical-historical witness Keil and Delitzsch lets the verse stand in its bare enormity within the catalogue: altars in the house of the LORD, the very place of which God had spoken so solemnly. The reformed John Gill, referring as throughout to the parallel at 2 Kings 21, reads it as one more stroke in the same account of Manasseh's idolatry. And the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the sense of all these verses into a single charge: Manasseh "profaned the house of God with his idolatry," turning the sanctuary of the living God into a shrine for the works of men's hands.

The witnesses do not divide, and the weight of the verse lies precisely in the clause the chronicler quotes back against the king. God had said his name should be in that house for ever; the promise of 2 Chronicles 7:16, that he had chosen and hallowed the temple that his name might be there perpetually, was the very charter of Jerusalem's holiness. To plant idol-altars there was not merely to sin but to insult the covenant, to answer God's "for ever" with a studied contempt. Ellicott fixes the Ahaz precedent and the heightened wording; Keil marks the naked fact; Henry names the profanation. Between them they show a king who did not keep his idolatry in the high places and the valleys but carried it into the holy place, defiling the one spot on earth God had set apart for his name, and so provoking, as the next verses will show, a wrath answerable to the outrage.
5:
The defilement of the temple deepens: Manasseh "built altars for all the host of heaven in the two courts of the house of the LORD." The witnesses read the verse as an intensifying of the sin just named, for now not one court but both are given over to the star-worship, and the whole enclosure of the sanctuary is turned into an observatory of idolatry. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, who had already identified "the host of heaven" as all the planets and stars, refers the principal facts of the chapter to the fuller notes on the parallel at 2 Kings 21, where the astral cult imported from Assyria and Babylon is set out at length. The altars in the two courts are altars to the sun, moon, and stars — the very lights God had made, now worshipped in the house of their Maker.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note the plain and dreadful fact: the altars were built for all the host of heaven in the two courts of the house of the LORD — the inner court of the priests and the great court of the people alike, so that no part of the sacred precinct was left undefiled. What had been the place of the LORD's worship became a place where the creature was adored in the face of the Creator. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry folds this with the verse before it into a single charge, that Manasseh "profaned God's chosen temple" and "debauched his chosen people" — the two courts, filled with strange altars, publishing his apostasy to every worshipper who entered.

The witnesses do not divide, and the horror of the verse lies in its geography. It was one thing to worship the host of heaven on the hills, as men had long done; it was another to erect altars to them within the courts where God had promised his name should dwell for ever. The astral religion of the great empires, with its careful attention to the movements of the stars, had crept into the very heart of Judah's worship, and the king who should have guarded the purity of the sanctuary had made it the seat of the corruption. Clarke names the deities and refers to the parallel; Keil marks the invasion of both courts; Henry the profaning of temple and people together. Between them they show the apostasy reaching its furthest extent within the walls of the house of God — the created lights of heaven adored where only their Maker had a right to be served, and the reader is prepared for the still darker abominations, of fire and divination, that the next verse will name.
6:
The abominations reach their nadir, and the witnesses trace the whole dark inventory the verse unrolls — child-sacrifice, augury, divination, sorcery, and traffic with the dead. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott gives the fullest reading. The plural "his children," he notes, is rhetorical, the older account at 2 Kings 21 speaking of "his son"; "in the valley of the son of Hinnom" is the chronicler's own explanatory addition, naming the notorious place of the fire-offering. Manasseh "observed times and used enchantments," which Ellicott renders "practised augury and divination" — forbidden at Leviticus 19:26 — the first term strictly meaning to observe clouds, the second to observe serpents; "used witchcraft" he takes as "muttered spells or charms"; and the dealing "with a familiar spirit and with wizards" he renders "appointed a necromancer and a wizard." The whole roll of soothsaying, he says, was drawn from Babylon; and, like Saul the first king of Israel before the witch of Endor, Manasseh appears to have despaired of any help or counsel from Jehovah and turned instead to the powers of darkness.

Ellicott sets the apostasy in its grim historical moment, borrowing the words of Robertson Smith: to all the nations under the Assyrian yoke the crisis had made careless confidence in their national gods impossible, so that "the darker aspects of heathenism became dominant. The wrath of the gods seemed more real than their favour; atoning ordinances were multiplied, human sacrifices became more frequent," and it was this terror-ridden face of heathenism that showed itself in Manasseh's imitations of foreign religion. The king "wrought much evil in the sight of the LORD" — literally, Ellicott observes, he "multiplied doing the evil," outdoing all his wicked predecessors.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry compresses the same catalogue into a single terrible line: Manasseh "dedicated his children to Moloch, and made the devil's lying oracles his guides and his counsellors." That is the heart of the verse's horror — a man forsaking the God who speaks truth for the demons who lie, and buying their favour with the blood of his own sons. The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott unfolds the philology of each forbidden art and the Assyrian dread that bred it; Henry names the two poles of the ruin, the murdered children and the consulted devils. Between them they show a king who had emptied his soul of God and filled it with terror, passing his sons through the fire in the valley of Hinnom and creeping after clouds and serpents and whispered spells for the guidance he would not seek from heaven. It is the portrait of apostasy come full circle — the covenant people's king become indistinguishable from the heathen whose abominations had once forfeited the land.
7:
Manasseh crowns his sacrilege by setting a carved image in the sanctuary, and the witnesses divide, mildly, over just what that image was. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reports that "he set up an image, the likeness of himself, in the house of the sanctuary," and adds that the Targumist supposes the king wished thereby to procure himself divine honours — a would-be god enthroned in the house of God. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the object differently: "he set the carven image of the idol which he had made," the word rendered "idol" (semel) explaining the "Asherah" of the older account at 2 Kings 21. Both terms, "carven image" and "idol," he notes, occur together in the law's own prohibition at Deuteronomy 4:16, so that the very words the chronicler chooses recall the statute Manasseh is breaking.

So a genuine, if small, difference stands between the witnesses over the identity of the image — whether it was a statue of the king himself, seeking worship (Clarke, following the Targum), or the image of Asherah, the fertility-goddess (Ellicott, from the parallel and the language of Deuteronomy). What neither doubts is where it was placed and what that placing meant. Ellicott presses the exactness of the chronicler's phrase: the image was set "in the house of God" — the word "of God" being the chronicler's own clarifying addition — and "the house" here denotes the Temple proper, the holy place itself, as distinct from the surrounding courts. The rare form rendered "for ever," he observes, occurs only here in the Hebrew of the Old Testament; God had said his name should be in this house for ever, and into that same house, "for ever" claimed by the LORD, Manasseh thrust his idol.

Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, let the verse stand as the summit of the temple-defilement, the graven image set where the ark and the cherubim proclaimed the invisible God who may not be imaged. The witnesses do not finally divide over the outrage, only over the figure that embodied it. Clarke and the Targum see a self-deifying king; Ellicott sees the goddess of the groves brought indoors; both see the second commandment trampled in the very sanctuary built to honour it. Between them they show idolatry reaching the innermost room of Judah's faith — a carved thing standing where God had promised his name should dwell, an image of the creature usurping the place of the God who forbids all images. It is the last and worst of Manasseh's sins against the house, and it is against this, as the closing verses will show, that his repentance will one day be measured, when with his own hands he casts the idol out.
8:
Against the mounting catalogue of sin the verse sets God's ancient promise, and the witnesses weigh both its terms and the covenant it recalls: God had said he would not "make the feet of Israel to move any more out of the land which I have appointed for your fathers; so that they will take heed to do all that I have commanded them." The whole security of Israel in the land, that is, hung upon obedience — a condition Manasseh had shattered at every point. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends closely to the wording. Where the chronicler writes "remove," the older account at 2 Kings 21 has the less common "cause to wander"; where he writes "the land which I appointed," Kings has the original "the land which I gave"; and the clause "so that," Ellicott renders "if only" — the promise is frankly conditional. The chronicler's "the statutes and the ordinances," he adds, is an explanatory expansion of Kings' "all the law that Moses my servant commanded them."

The most pointed of Ellicott's notes falls on the phrase "by the hand of Moses." This is the chronicler's characteristic interpretation, he says, of what stands in the parallel at 2 Kings 21:8; and it is careful theology, for it notes that the authority of the Lawgiver was not primary but derived. Moses gave the law by his hand, but the law was God's; the commandments Manasseh spurned were not a prophet's counsel but the LORD's own charge, mediated through his servant. To break them was to break with God directly.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the verse against the enormity of the king's contempt: Manasseh sinned "in contempt of the choice God had made of Sion to be his rest for ever and Israel to be his covenant-people." The promise of an unmoved dwelling in the land was bound to the election of Zion as God's rest — the very rest of which the psalmist sings — and to the covenant that made Israel God's own; and Manasseh trampled all of it, forfeiting by his apostasy the security the promise had offered. The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott secures the conditional force of the promise, the chronicler's careful hand upon his source, and the derived authority of Moses; Henry names the covenant privileges — Zion chosen for God's rest, Israel chosen for his people — that the king despised. Between them they show why the sin was so grave: God had pledged to keep Israel unmoved in the land, but only while they kept his commandments, and Manasseh had loaded the scale with every abomination the law forbade. The promise that might have secured the kingdom becomes, in his hands, the measure of its coming exile.
9:
The indictment closes on the corporate ruin the king had wrought: "Manasseh made Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem to err, and to do worse than the heathen, whom the LORD had destroyed before the children of Israel." The sin is no longer Manasseh's alone; he has dragged a whole people down with him, and to a depth below that of the very nations God had exterminated to make room for Israel. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the verse literally — "Manasseh led Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem astray, to do evil more than the nations" — and reports a source-critical observation of the critic Thenius, who thought the words "and Manasseh led astray" once followed in the primary document immediately upon "he set the graven image in the house," the intervening clauses being an addition by the editor of the older account. Whether or not that reconstruction stands, the sense is plain: the king who had defiled the temple now seduced the nation.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry fastens on the dreadful comparative — worse than the heathen — and reaches for the Lord's own image of relapse: "He made them to err, and do worse than the heathen; for if the unclean spirit returns, he brings with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself." Judah had been swept and garnished under Hezekiah, the demons of idolatry cast out; and now, the house standing empty of true devotion, the unclean spirit returns with sevenfold reinforcement, so that the last state is worse than the first. A people who had known the true God and forsaken him sink lower than a people who never knew him at all.

The reformed John Gill, reading throughout with an eye on the parallel at 2 Kings 21, takes the verse as the summary of the whole apostasy there recorded — the seduction of Judah being the bitter fruit of the king's own example. The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott secures the literal force and reports Thenius's textual conjecture; Henry presses the terrible logic of relapse, worse than the heathen because privileged above them; Gill anchors the whole in the older history. Between them they show the final aggravation of Manasseh's guilt: that he was not content to ruin himself but ruined his people, teaching Judah and Jerusalem to outdo in wickedness the Canaanites whom God had destroyed. It is this national corruption, more than any private crime, that draws down the judgment of the verses that follow — for a king may answer for his own sins, but a king who makes a nation to sin answers for theirs as well.
10:
Before judgment falls, mercy speaks: "the LORD spake to Manasseh, and to his people: but they would not hearken." The witnesses dwell on the grace of the warning and the guilt of the refusal. The reformed John Gill notes simply that God spoke by his servants the prophets, whose message is recorded in the older account. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fills in that substance from the parallel at 2 Kings 21:10-15, where the prophetic sentence against Manasseh is given at length; and he adds the terrible detail the chronicler had noted, that Manasseh "shed very much innocent blood, till he had filled Jerusalem from one end to the other." The reaction against Hezekiah's reforms, Ellicott judges, had ended in a bloody struggle in which the party of reform was fiercely suppressed — the prophets who carried God's word being among the martyrs of that persecution.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the verse a meditation on the meeting of divine patience and human obstinacy. God spoke to Manasseh and his people by the prophets, "but they would not hearken." Here, Henry says, we may admire at once the grace of God in speaking to them and their hardness in turning a deaf ear: either their badness did not quite turn away his goodness, for still he waited to be gracious, or his goodness did not turn them from their badness, for still they hated to be reformed. The warning was itself a mercy — God does not strike the sinner without first calling him — and the refusal of the warning is the very thing that seals the sinner's guilt.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch draw the line straight from this refusal to the stroke that follows: because Manasseh would not hear the words of the prophets, the LORD brought upon him the captains of the host of the king of Assyria. The prophetic word rejected becomes the Assyrian sword invited. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott fix the messengers and the bloody setting in which they spoke; Henry weighs the grace of the speaking against the obstinacy of the hearing; Keil marks the causal hinge, the deaf ear that summons the invader. Between them they show that Manasseh's judgment was not arbitrary but earned — God had held out his hand all the day long to a disobedient and gainsaying people, and only when the word was spurned and the prophets silenced did the captains of Assyria appear on the horizon. The mercy of the warning is the measure of the justice of the blow.
11:
The judgment arrives in the shape of the Assyrian army, and the witnesses gather around both the identity of the captor and the vivid phrase "among the thorns." The reformed John Gill names the great king as Esarhaddon, son and successor of Sennacherib, and dates the captivity, by the Jewish chronology, to the twenty-second year of Manasseh's reign. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott is more cautious about the king: the captains were the generals of Esarhaddon, or rather perhaps of Assurbanipal, and he cites the Assyrian inscriptions in which "Menasseh king of Judah" is listed among the tributary kings of both monarchs, so that Manasseh paid tribute to father and son alike. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley explains why the Babylonian conqueror is here styled "king of Assyria" — because he had added Assyria to his empire — and traces the invasion to greed and opportunity: informed by the ambassadors of the treasures at Jerusalem and assured of Manasseh's departure from his father's God, the king judged this a fit season to strike.

Over the phrase "took Manasseh among the thorns" a real difference of reading opens. Keil and Delitzsch reject both "in the thorns" and a supposed place called Chochim, and render it "they took him with hooks" — the hook or ring drawn through the gills of a great fish at Job 41:2, or through the nose of a wild beast at 2 Kings 19:28 and Ezekiel 19:4; Manasseh is figured as an unmanageable beast subdued by a ring in the nose. Ellicott agrees that the hooks might be those the Assyrian kings passed through the lips of their distinguished prisoners, comparing the LORD's threat to Sennacherib at Isaiah 37:29 and the fish-hooks of Amos 4:2; yet he allows a second possibility, that the word is a local name, "at Hohim." The fetters he takes for the double chain of bronze with which the Philistines bound Samson at Judges 16:21. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads "among the thorns" a third way, figuratively: Manasseh was perplexed in his counsels and embarrassed in his affairs — as we say, "in the briers" — and so became an easy prey; bound now with iron who had long been held with the cords of his own iniquity, and carried to Babylon, that the treasures Hezekiah's pride had shown off might become the invader's spoil, as Isaiah had foretold.

The witnesses do not divide over the substance — a proud king seized, chained, and dragged to Babylon — only over the picture in the word. Gill and Wesley name Esarhaddon and his motive; Ellicott weighs Esarhaddon against Assurbanipal and cites the inscriptions; Keil and Ellicott read the hooks of a captured beast, while Henry hears the briers of a man ensnared. Between them they show the hand of God in the Assyrian's, chastising a sinful people and subduing a straying prince by the very empire whose favour his idols could not buy.
12:
In the depth of his affliction Manasseh turns at last to God, and the witnesses read the verse as the great hinge of the chapter — the proud idolater humbled into a penitent. The reformed John Gill fixes the setting: the king was in prison, or at least in fetters, and a Jewish tradition, echoed by an Arabian writer, told of a brazen instrument bored full of holes in which he was confined with fire kindled about it, a device like the brazen bull of Perillus. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke relays the same Chaldee legend more fully — the Chaldeans made a brazen mule pierced with small holes, put him within it, and lit fires all around; and in that misery he first sought help of all the idols he had made, and finding none, repented and prayed before the LORD his God.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch turn from the legend to the text: in his distress Manasseh besought the LORD and humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers — the same construction, they note, as the affliction of Ahaz at 2 Chronicles 28:22, though with the opposite issue, for where Ahaz in his distress trespassed yet more, Manasseh bowed. The prayer he prayed, they add, was recorded in the histories of the kings and in the sayings of the seer, but has not come down to us. Charles Ellicott, of the same school, presses the philology: "besought" is literally "stroked the face," the vivid realistic phrase that meets us at Exodus 32:11; and he marks the pathos of the object, "the God of his fathers" — the very God whom Manasseh had forsaken for the gods of aliens, now sought again in the extremity.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the lesson the scene enforces: it becomes sinners to humble themselves before the God whom they have offended, and sufferers to humble themselves before him who corrects them, and to accept the punishment of their iniquity. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Clarke preserve the tradition of the brazen prison; Keil and Ellicott fix the sincerity of the humbling and the tenderness of "the God of his fathers"; Wesley reads the moral of penitent submission. Between them they show that affliction, which had hardened Ahaz, softened Manasseh — that the same fire may temper one man and consume another, and that the difference lies not in the furnace but in whether the sufferer, stripped of his idols and finding them helpless, turns his face at last toward the God he had despised.
13:
The prayer is answered, and the witnesses marvel at the completeness of the mercy: God "was intreated of him, and heard his supplication, and brought him again to Jerusalem into his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the LORD he was God." The reformed John Gill reads the prayer plainly as a cry for mercy and forgiveness, granted. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that God heard and restored him to his kingdom, and Charles Ellicott sets the restoration in its historical light: the Assyrian monarch, after a time, saw fit to reinstate Manasseh as a vassal king — a case, Ellicott observes, exactly parallel to that of the Egyptian king Necho, who was bound and sent to Nineveh and afterwards restored by Assurbanipal to his former state. The closing words, "that the LORD he was God," Ellicott compares to the cry of the people at Carmel in 1 Kings 18:39, where the same Hebrew stands; and the being "intreated of him" he links to 1 Chronicles 5:20.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke relays at length the Jewish legend of the deliverance, and weighs it honestly. The Targum tells how the presiding angels shut all the gates and windows of heaven that his prayer might not enter, until the compassions of the Creator moved him to make a window under the throne of his glory, through which he heard the supplication; how at his word the earth shook and the brazen prison burst, and the Spirit from between the cherubim returned the king to Jerusalem, where he knew that the LORD was God and served his idols no more. Clarke calls the tale curious and in part childish, yet reckons that beneath such fancies the ancient rabbins purposely hid deep and important meanings.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the theology of the whole restoration. God, being entreated, made a way for the king's escape; and afflictions, Henry observes, are continued no longer than till they have done their work — when Manasseh is brought back to his God and his duty, he is soon brought back to his kingdom. See here, he urges, how ready God is to accept and welcome returning sinners, and how swift to show mercy: let no great sinner despair, when Manasseh himself found favour; in him God showed forth a pattern of long-suffering, as at 1 Timothy 1:16 and Isaiah 1:18. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the prayer for pardon, Keil and Ellicott the restoration and the historical parallel that vouches for it, Clarke the rabbinic legend and its hidden sense, Henry the swift and welcoming grace. Between them they show the crowning wonder of the chapter — that the arch-idolater of Judah's kings, dragged in chains to Babylon, was heard, forgiven, and set again upon his throne, a living proof that no sinner is beyond the reach of pardoning mercy who will but turn and pray.
14:
Restored to his throne, Manasseh sets about repairing what his sin had exposed, and the witnesses read the building of the wall as the visible fruit of his repentance. He "built a wall without the city of David, on the west side of Gihon, in the valley, even to the entering in at the fish gate, and compassed about Ophel, and raised it up a very great height." The reformed John Gill supposes this wall had been broken down by the Assyrian army when it took the city, and, citing Vitringa, identifies it with the old wall by the pool of Siloah. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it likewise as a weak place newly fortified, or a stretch of wall the Assyrians had thrown down and Manasseh now rebuilt.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the work in its full topography and draws from its very exactness an argument for its truth. Manasseh, he says, completed the outer wall that Hezekiah had begun at 2 Chronicles 32:5, carrying it westward to Gihon and round by the fish gate that lay near the north-east corner of the lower city, as at Nehemiah 3:3; he surrounded the Ophel mound, on which Uzziah and Jotham had already laboured at 2 Chronicles 26:9 and 2 Chronicles 27:3, and raised the whole to a great height, setting captains of war in the fenced cities. This highly circumstantial account of his public works, Ellicott judges, is utterly unlike fiction and almost compels the assumption of a real historical source, no longer extant, from which the section is drawn. His fellow grammatical-historical witness Keil and Delitzsch reads the words as pointing to a new outer wall, and canvasses the question whether it be identical with the wall Hezekiah had built.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the masonry into a parable. It was sin, he observes, that had ruined the king; and now that he returned to God in the way of duty, God returned to him in the way of mercy, and he built a wall about the city of David — "for by sin he had unwalled it and exposed it to the enemy." He set captains of war in the fenced cities for the security of his country, and, as Josephus reports, all the rest of his days was so changed for the better that he was reckoned a happy man. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Clarke fix the breach and its repair; Ellicott traces the wall's exact course and finds in its detail the mark of genuine history; Keil weighs its relation to Hezekiah's; Henry reads in the rebuilt wall the outward sign of an inward restoration. Between them they show a penitent king shoring up the defences his rebellion had breached, and teach that true repentance does not rest in feeling but labours to repair the ruin sin has made.
15:
The clearest evidence of the king's changed heart is the purging of the idols he had once enthroned, and the witnesses mark the reversal with satisfaction. Manasseh "took away the strange gods, and the idol out of the house of the LORD, and all the altars that he had built in the mount of the house of the LORD, and in Jerusalem, and cast them out of the city." The reformed John Gill notes plainly that he removed the strange gods and the idol he had set in the temple. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch specify the scope: he cleared the idols and statues out of the two courts of the temple and caused the idolatrous altars he had built on the temple hill and in the city to be cast forth beyond the walls.

Charles Ellicott, of the same school, fixes the terms and adds a candid limit. The "strange gods" (elohe nekar) are the foreign deities of Genesis 35:2; "the idol" is the Asherah he had set in the house; the altars stood "in the mount of the house," which Thenius takes of the temple courts. Yet the reform, Ellicott observes, was hardly complete, for some of Manasseh's altars remained for Josiah to pull down at 2 Kings 23:12 — a note that will matter greatly when the next reign revives what this one only partly removed. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the whole action as the proof of a real conversion: Manasseh appears to have done everything in his power to destroy the idolatry he had set up and to restore the pure worship of the true God, so that his repentance brought forth fruits meet for repentance.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the inward turn behind the outward act. Now, he trusts, the king loathed the idols as much as ever he had loved them, and said to them, "Get you hence — what have I to do any more with idols? I have had enough of them." Repentance, for Henry, is not complete in sorrow; it turns from the sin, and Manasseh turns from his by casting his gods over the wall. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the removal, Keil the clearing of the courts and city, Ellicott the identity of the idols and the incompleteness that left work for Josiah, Clarke the fruits of a true conversion, Henry the loathing that replaced the old love. Between them they show a penitent undoing his own apostasy with his own hands — the man who had carried the idol into the sanctuary now carrying it out again, and teaching every later reader that the surest test of a changed heart is a changed practice, and that the idols we once welcomed we must be willing, at last, to cast out of the city altogether.
16:
Having cleared away the false worship, Manasseh restores the true, and the witnesses attend to a textual nicety in the verb and a larger question behind it. He "repaired the altar of the LORD, and sacrificed thereon peace offerings and thank offerings, and commanded Judah to serve the LORD God of Israel." The reformed John Gill notes that the altar had fallen to ruin, neglected and disused through the years of idolatry; or, by the marginal reading which the Targum follows, that Manasseh "built" it, having perhaps before pulled it down. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch record the same variant — some manuscripts and old editions read that he "prepared" the altar rather than "built" it, a difference perhaps born of an orthographic slip — and reason that Manasseh had not likely removed the altar of the LORD and then restored it, for its removal would surely have been mentioned earlier in the catalogue of his sins.

Charles Ellicott, of the same school, weighs the same reading and reports the bolder inference of Ewald, who concluded from the word "built" that Manasseh had indeed torn down the altar of burnt offering, and from the silence of Jeremiah 3:16 about the ark that he had destroyed the ark of the covenant as well. Ellicott himself judges the reading "prepared," supported by the Syriac and Arabic, to be doubtless right. So a genuine, if quiet, debate runs beneath the verb: had Manasseh in his apostasy actually demolished the altar (and even the ark), so that "built" is literal, or did he merely repair and re-consecrate an altar long neglected? Keil and Ellicott lean to the milder reading; Ewald presses the harsher.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry passes over the philology to the pastoral point. Manasseh "returned to his duty," repairing the altar and offering upon it peace offerings to implore God's favour and thank offerings to praise him for his deliverance; and, having once abused his power to corrupt his people, he now used it to reform them, commanding Judah to serve the LORD God of Israel. Those who truly repent, Henry observes, will not only return to God themselves but do all they can to recover those whom their example had drawn away, that they may make the plaster as wide as the wound. The witnesses do not divide over the restoration itself. Gill and Keil fix the ruined and repaired altar; Ellicott and Ewald dispute how far the ruin had gone; Henry reads the double offering and the royal command as the mark of a repentance that labours to undo the harm it once did. Between them they show a king turning his authority inside out — the hand that had commanded idolatry now commanding the worship of the true God, and the reader taught that genuine penitence is never content to save itself, but seeks to heal the wound it opened in others.
17:
The reformation, real as it was, did not reach all the way, and the witnesses weigh the qualification the verse records: "Nevertheless the people did sacrifice still in the high places, yet unto the LORD their God only." The reformed John Gill fixes the limit precisely — the people still sacrificed on the high places, but not now to the idols; their worship was directed to the LORD, though offered in the wrong place. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke confirms the sense from the Targum, which reads that they sacrificed on the high places "but only to the name of the Word of the LORD their God." The idolatry was gone; the irregularity remained.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch let the notice stand as it is — the high places tolerated, but the worship on them now rendered to the LORD alone — a half-measure that fell short of the law's demand for one central sanctuary, yet was no longer the apostasy of the earlier verses. The distinction matters: the sin of Manasseh's youth had been the worship of false gods; the fault that lingered was the worship of the true God in unlawful places, a lesser evil but an evil still, and one that later reforms would have to address.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the lesson the verse quietly teaches: "Manasseh could not carry the reformation so far as he had carried the corruption. It is an easy thing to debauch men's manners, but not so easy to reform them again." Here is the sober arithmetic of sin and repentance — a king may plunge a people into idolatry in a few years, but he cannot lift them wholly out of it even by a lifetime of penitent labour; the habits he taught outlive the teacher's change of heart. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, tracing the same thread, notes that Manasseh prevailed to bring the people off from their false gods but not from their high places; the deeper the corruption had struck root, the harder it proved to pull up altogether. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Clarke fix the residual worship as directed now to the LORD only; Keil marks it as a half-reform short of the law; Wesley and Henry read the melancholy lesson that corruption is sooner spread than cured. Between them they show a reformation genuine but incomplete — the idols cast out, the true God owned, yet the old habits of place not wholly broken — and they leave the reader with the warning that sin, once made popular, leaves a sediment that even sincere repentance may not entirely sweep away.
18:
The historian begins to close the reign, and the witnesses attend to the sources he names and the honour the record does to the king's prayer: "the rest of the acts of Manasseh, and his prayer unto his God, and the words of the seers that spake to him in the name of the LORD God of Israel, behold, they are written in the book of the kings of Israel." The reformed John Gill notes that this covers all his acts, good and bad, before and after his conversion. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott identifies the compiler's authorities: the words of the seers, first mentioned earlier in the chapter, were incorporated in the great history of the kings, one of the chronicler's principal sources; the word "written," though wanting in the present Hebrew, is read in some manuscripts and in the versions; and the parallel notice at 2 Kings 21:17 refers, as usual, to the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.

Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, distinguish the sources more finely still: the other acts of Manasseh, his prayer, and the words of the prophets against him were recorded in the history of the kings of Israel, while the special accounts of his prayer and its hearing, of his sons, and of the high places and images he had raised before his humbling, were contained in the sayings of the seer. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley clears up the puzzling phrase "the book of the kings of Israel," explaining that "Israel" here means Judah, often so called; the reference is not to the canonical book of Kings, where these things are not found, but to the public records from which the prophets drew the most important matters for the sacred history.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks the striking prominence the record gives to Manasseh's repentance. The heads of his history, for which we are referred to the other writings, are more than of any of the kings; and among them a particular account was kept of his prayer, twice mentioned as a remarkable thing, and of how God was entreated of him — written, Henry says, for the generations to come, that the people yet to be created might praise the LORD for his readiness to receive returning prodigals. Notice too, Henry adds, that account was kept of the words of the seers who spoke to him, that men might consider how a reckoning is made of the warnings God sends. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the compass of the acts, Ellicott and Keil the several documentary sources, Wesley the sense of "Israel," Henry the honour done to the prayer of a penitent. Between them they show a chronicler who, having recorded the worst of Manasseh, is careful to record the best — that the penitence of a great sinner should stand on the sacred page as a lasting encouragement to every prodigal who reads it.
19:
The historian dwells once more on the prayer and the sins it repented of, and the witnesses fasten chiefly on the disputed name of the record that preserved it: "his prayer also, and how God was intreated of him, and all his sin, and his trespass, and the places wherein he built high places... before he was humbled: behold, they are written among the sayings of the seers." The reformed John Gill notes that the prayer was recorded not only in the royal annals but in the writings of another named afterward. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch summarize the contents — the prayer, its hearing, all the sin and trespass, and the high places, groves, and images set up before the king was humbled — as gathered in the sayings of the seer.

Over that seer's name a real difference opens. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reports the readings faithfully: the Targum and Vulgate give "the words of Chozai," treating it as a proper name; the Syriac names the prophet Hunan, the Arabic Saphan. Charles Ellicott, of the grammatical-historical school, presses past the versions to a judgment: "Hozai," he argues, is pretty clearly a mutilated form of ha-hozim, "the seers" — the very term used earlier in the chapter — so that the phrase means not the sayings of a prophet called Hozai but the sayings of the seers in general. So the witnesses genuinely divide: was the source the memoir of a particular seer, Hozai (or Hunan, or Saphan, as the versions variously guessed), or is "Hozai" simply a corruption of the plural "the seers"?

Ellicott adds the chronicler's characteristic heightening of the language: where the older account at 2 Kings 21:17 has only "his sin that he sinned," the chronicler writes "all his sin and his unfaithfulness"; and the "groves" are the Asherim of the earlier verses. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the careful listing of the sins "before he was humbled" as itself a fruit of the king's penitence — the account being probably taken from his own confession, which he left upon record, taking shame to himself and giving thanks to the reprovers who had warned him. The witnesses do not divide over the substance of the record, only over the name that heads it. Gill and Keil fix its contents; Clarke gathers the versions' guesses; Ellicott argues the name away into "the seers"; Henry reads the whole as the humble self-accusation of a pardoned man. Between them they show a penitent willing to have his own sins written down for the warning of others, and a chronicler preserving, under whatever name, the memoir in which a great sinner's fall and rising were faithfully told.
20:
The reign ends with the customary formula, but the witnesses catch a note of quiet difference in the place of the king's burial: "So Manasseh slept with his fathers, and they buried him in his own house: and Amon his son reigned in his stead." The reformed John Gill explains "in his own house" of the garden of his house, and gathers the burial customs around it: the Jews in later times buried in gardens, and it was the way of the ancients, Greeks and Romans alike, to bury their dead within their own dwellings, whence sprang the worship of the household gods, the Lares and Penates. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the reading from the parallel: the older account at 2 Kings 21:18 says he was buried "in the garden of his house, in the garden of Uzza," and the words "in the garden of" seem to have fallen out of the chronicler's text, as the Septuagint and Syriac attest.

Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, confirm the more exact statement of Kings — that Manasseh was buried in the garden of his house, the garden of Uzza — and carry the narrative forward to the accession of Amon. The point on which the grammatical-historical witnesses agree is that the burial was not in the royal sepulchres of the kings but in a private garden-tomb, a departure from the usual honour.

That departure is precisely what the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads with a moral eye. Manasseh was buried, he notes, not in the sepulchres of the kings but in his own house; he was buried privately, and nothing of the honour was done him at his death that had been done to his godly father Hezekiah. And Henry finds in this a gentle justice tempered with hope: "Penitents may recover their comfort sooner than their credit." The pardoned king had found peace with God, but the marks of his long apostasy clung to his name even in the grave; forgiveness was complete, but reputation is a slower thing to heal. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the garden-burial and its ancient customs, Ellicott and Keil the dropped words and the garden of Uzza, Henry the diminished honour and its lesson. Between them they show a repentant king laid to rest without the full pomp of his fathers — a man truly forgiven, yet bearing to his tomb the shadow of the sins he had repented of, and teaching that while God restores the penitent's comfort at once, the world is slower to restore his credit, and some consequences of sin outlast even sincere repentance.
21:
The narrative turns to Manasseh's son, and the witnesses treat the brief accession-notice — "Amon was two and twenty years old when he began to reign, and reigned two years in Jerusalem" — as the sober opening of a reign that will be all the darker for following so bright a repentance. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch compare the two records and find them agreeing, save that the chronicle, as with Manasseh and Ahaz before, omits the name of the king's mother and gives a somewhat briefer account of his godless deeds, while adding the pointed remark that Amon did not humble himself as his father had but increased his guilt. In the notice of his death, they observe, the chronicle says nothing of his burial nor refers to the sources of his history — a silence that itself marks how little there was to tell.

The other grammatical-historical witness, Charles Ellicott, notes that the age given, two and twenty years, agrees with the parallel at 2 Kings 21:19, which adds the mother's name and parentage that the chronicler passes over. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, marking the two-year reign, simply refers the reader to the fuller notes on the same parallel. The chronicler's economy — the omitted mother, the abbreviated record, the unmentioned burial-place — is not accidental but of a piece with his manner, reserving his fuller attention for the reigns that carried weight for the history of true worship, and hurrying over a king whose brief rule added nothing but sin.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry catches the tone exactly in his opening word on the reign: "We have little recorded concerning Amon, but enough, unless it were better." A short life and a bad one leave the historian little to say, and what there is, is not worth the saying except as a warning. The witnesses do not divide. Keil and Ellicott fix the age and the chronicler's characteristic omissions; Clarke refers to the parallel; Henry sets the melancholy key. Between them they show a young king of two and twenty mounting the throne his penitent father had left, and the reader is made to feel, in the very brevity of the record, the contrast that the following verses will draw out — a son who had before his eyes the most memorable repentance in all the book of the kings, and would not learn from it. The stage is set, in a few bare words, for a tragedy of squandered example.
22:
Amon's character is fixed in a sentence, and the witnesses press the astonishing fact that a son should copy his father's sins while ignoring his father's repentance: "he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, as did Manasseh his father: for Amon sacrificed unto all the carved images which Manasseh his father had made, and served them." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as the summary of a reign that reproduced Manasseh's idolatry without Manasseh's turning. Charles Ellicott presses the wording and its implication: the older account at 2 Kings 21 says Amon "served the idols that his father served," using a term of contempt the chronicler avoids; and the statement that Amon sacrificed to "the carved images which Manasseh had made" seems to imply that those images had not been destroyed but only cast aside — though Ellicott cautions, against the critic Reuss, that this casts no doubt on the reality of Manasseh's reform, for the words need not mean the very images the penitent father had discarded, but only images of the same imaginary gods.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry seizes on that same point and turns it into a lesson on the law's severity. Those who think Amon's relapse proves that Manasseh never truly repented, Henry says, forget how many good men have had wicked sons. But he grants a real defect in Manasseh's reform: when he cast out the images he did not utterly deface and destroy them, as the law at Deuteronomy 7:2 required Israel to burn the images with fire; and so the carved images, only thrown by and not burnt, lay ready to Amon's hand, who knew where to find them and soon set them up again. How necessary that law was, Henry observes, this instance shows.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke voices the plain astonishment of the scene: "How astonishing is this! with his father's example before his eyes, he copies his father's vices, but not his repentance." The son had the whole memorable history — the apostasy, the chains, the humbling, the pardon, the reform — set before him as in a mirror, and he chose to imitate only the sin. The witnesses do not divide. Keil fixes the reproduced idolatry; Ellicott presses the images that were cast aside rather than destroyed, guarding Manasseh's repentance against Reuss; Henry finds in the undestroyed images the vindication of the law that commanded their burning; Clarke names the wonder of a son who copied the vice and refused the penitence. Between them they show a young king willfully squandering the costliest example a father ever left, and teach that reformation which merely lays sin aside, without destroying it root and branch, leaves the seed of relapse for the next generation to find.
23:
The verse names the fatal difference between father and son — not that Amon sinned, but that he would not repent: "he humbled not himself before the LORD, as Manasseh his father had humbled himself; but Amon trespassed more and more." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it as the mark of a man who took no warning: Amon appears to have exceeded his father in wickedness and would learn nothing from his father's fall or his father's rising. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that this verse is the chronicler's own addition, absent from the parallel, and renders the last clause literally, "for he, Amon, multiplied trespass" — a deliberate heaping-up of guilt. Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, set the contrast in its starkest form: where Manasseh humbled himself, Amon did not, but increased his guilt the more.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the theology out with unusual force. Amon came short of his father not in sinning but in repenting: "He fell like him, but did not get up again like him." And here Henry lays bare the true ground of ruin: "It is not so much sin as impenitence in sin that ruins men — not so much that they offend, as that they do not humble themselves for their offences; not the disease, but the neglect of the remedy." Manasseh had sinned deeply, yet was saved, because he humbled himself and sought the cure; Amon sinned and was lost, because he despised it. The difference between the pardoned father and the perishing son was not the greatness of the guilt but the presence or absence of penitence.

Henry sharpens the warning against a presumption the young king may well have nursed. Perhaps Amon, sinning as his father had in his early days, promised himself that he would repent as his father had in his latter days; but his case shows what madness it is to presume upon that, for he was cut off in his sins while still young, and never got the old age he counted on. The witnesses do not divide. Clarke and Ellicott fix the multiplied trespass and the chronicler's own emphasis; Keil marks the bare contrast of humbling and hardening; Henry unfolds the doctrine that impenitence, not sin alone, destroys. Between them they show the whole tragedy of Amon in a single antithesis — a father who fell and rose, a son who fell and lay still — and press upon every reader the lesson that the door of mercy which stood open to the worst of penitents stands shut against none but those who, like Amon, will not stoop to enter it.
24:
Amon's reign is cut short by violence, and the witnesses read the swift end as at once a human crime and a divine judgment: "his servants conspired against him, and slew him in his own house." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke confesses the limits of the record — on what account the servants conspired, he says, we cannot tell; the motive is left in darkness. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch simply set down the fact within the close of the reign: the servants conspired and slew the king in his own house, the same house, perhaps, in which his father had been buried.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the death its moral weight, reading it against the presumption of the verse before. Amon reigned but two years, and then his own servants turned on him. Perhaps, Henry suggests, when Amon sinned as his father had in his youth he promised himself that he too should repent in his age; but if he hoped to repent when he was old, he was wretchedly disappointed, for he was cut off while young. And Henry marks the fit retribution in the manner of it: "He rebelled against God, and his own servants rebelled against him." The king who would not submit to his heavenly Lord found his own subjects refusing submission to him; the treachery he had shown to God was answered by the treachery of his household. In this, Henry insists, God was righteous, though the conspirators were wicked — the murder was a sin in them and a judgment on him at once.

The witnesses do not divide, and the brevity of the notice is itself eloquent. Clarke owns that the conspirators' reasons are unknown; Keil fixes the bare fact of the assassination in the royal house; Henry reads the providence beneath the crime — a young king cut off in his impenitence, his own servants the rod, his own rebellion the reason. Between them they show the abrupt closing of a reign that had squandered every warning: the son who would not humble himself before the LORD is struck down in his own palace before he is well seated on his throne, and the reader is left to weigh the terrible symmetry Henry names, that the man who rebels against God may find, in his own house, rebels enough to bring him down. The presumption of a distant repentance is answered by a sudden and violent death, and the door Amon meant to enter "later" is shut upon him for ever.
25:
The chapter ends with the people avenging the murdered king and setting his son upon the throne: "the people of the land slew all them that had conspired against king Amon; and the people of the land made Josiah his son king in his stead." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the popular reaction shrewdly: the murder of Amon was no popular act, for the people slew the regicides — and yet, he adds, the people were themselves as prone to idolatry as their king had been, so that their vengeance was for the crime against the crown, not zeal for any righteousness. Clarke rests satisfied, too, that idolatry in that age was bound up with licentiousness and sensual gratification, else as a mere system of religion it could never have held such sway over the nation.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch record the close of the matter plainly — the people of the land put the conspirators to death and made Josiah, Amon's son, king in his stead — and so the succession passed, past the murdered father, to the child who would prove the last great reformer of Judah. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the justice of the execution: rightly, he says, did the people of the land put the conspirators to death as traitors, for the lives of kings are particularly under the protection of Providence and of the laws both of God and man. The assassination of Amon, wicked as the king was, was still a crime against the divinely-guarded order of the throne, and the nation was right to punish it.

So the chapter that opened with the worst of Judah's kings closes with the accession of one of the best. The witnesses do not divide. Clarke reads the mixed motives of a people who avenged their king yet clung to their idols; Keil fixes the succession to Josiah; Henry vindicates the punishment of the traitors under the providence that guards the throne. Between them they show the strange mercy that runs beneath the violence: out of the murder of an impenitent idolater God brings forth, in the boy Josiah, the instrument of Judah's last and greatest reformation. The line of David, so nearly wrecked by two generations of apostasy and one of them unrepented, is preserved and turned again toward the LORD, and the reader who has followed Manasseh's fall and rising, and Amon's fall without rising, is left to see the covenant faithfulness of God quietly securing, through crime and vengeance alike, the throne on which a better king shall sit.
